about.heading: About
about.headline: Most people do one part of this. Caio does the span.
about.bio:
Caio Ogata is a Creative Designer. A former art director with a background in user interfaces and a self-taught path into development. He is happiest building sites that tell a story the way a photograph does. Through what you see and feel, rather than by explaining themselves.

Cinema and photography came first, years before either was work. Framing, composition, colour, the way a shot moves. Technology ran alongside them, in video games and computers, and it is the more logical half of how he thinks. Advertising was where the looking became work.

Nothing on the screen is there by accident. Type, grid, motion and interaction all do a job, and they get decided together. He designs the experience and writes the code that makes it behave.

The craft comes from advertising. Several years in agencies as an art director, then a specialisation at Miami Ad School in São Paulo. The discipline there is making an idea land in a single look.

Huia is where the two halves met. He joined the creative technology studio in 2013 and stayed eight years, six of them as partner. The brief was rarely a layout. It was a question: can this be built? The answers ran on WebGL, facial recognition and machine learning, years before any of that was ordinary. He led creative direction for Petrobras, O Boticário, Tramontina, Sicredi and Mondelez brands. He also picked up the habit he still works by, which is to build a rough one early and look at it.

Azion Technologies hired him to build a design operation from nothing, inside a company of engineers. He grew it to fourteen people across five disciplines. Four years, three roles: design, then brand, then the tools engineers use. Sitting that close to engineering taught him the other half of the job. How software actually ships, what a component costs, why an engineer says no.

Most people who do this work do one part of it. Caio does the span. The idea, the way it looks, and the thing that actually runs. For a client that means one person from start to finish.

items.title: Lukso
items.description: The website of a story-first agency that works for Disney, PepsiCo and Ambev. Lukso's work was bold, colourful and full of movement, and its old site did not show it. The new one makes that impression on the first scroll.
items.technologies: Next.js, React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, GSAP, Lenis, Tailwind CSS, Vercel
items.impact: A bilingual single page where visitors stay longer, with twelve custom 3D icons and one template behind thirteen case pages. Structured data and llms.txt files let search engines and AI assistants find and describe the agency. Caio designed and built it through COLABS, from the first layout to the live site.

sections.body: A single page that makes the first impression Lukso's work already makes: bold, moving, and told as a story.

sections.challenge: Lukso has strong cases, big clients and a clear position: story first. Its work is bold, animated and full of colour. Its website was not, and a visitor had to dig before seeing what the agency can deliver.
sections.solution: One page that walks through the agency in order. It opens on "What's your story?" and the story-first promise. The reel comes right after, jumping to the middle of the screen over a moving background. Then the four pillars and the work inside each one, followed by clients, cases, the team and a call for new clients.

sections.body: Dark by default, with amber used like punctuation, so the strongest colour on screen comes from Lukso's own work.

features.name: Opening
features.description: A yellow curtain lifts and the headline assembles around three 3D icons: a magnifying glass, a play button and a star.

features.name: Four pillars
features.description: Narrative, Content, Culture and Training, each with the kinds of work Lukso delivers inside it. The section holds on screen while each 3D icon turns into the next.

features.name: Cases

items.title: Azion Website & Brand Expansion
items.description: Azion changed how it describes itself: from an edge computing platform to a web platform for modern workloads. The website had to carry that change across dozens of products that, until then, all looked alike.
items.technologies: Astro, Vue.js, Design Tokens, Webkit Component Library, Storybook, Sora, Monospace Type, Technical Illustration
items.impact: One system behind 19 product pages, 6 solution pages, the documentation and the console. Product, documentation and support teams fix and publish on their own, and a new idea reaches preview in about four hours. Live since Q3 2025, and still growing.

sections.body: A brand repositioning, told through the website. Fewer abstract promises, more drawings of how the product actually works.

sections.challenge: Azion was moving away from "edge computing platform", a category the market had not fully adopted. The website could not carry the new story. Dozens of products were hard to explain, a short palette made every page look like the last, and the illustrations described the products in terms too abstract for a developer.
sections.solution: The brand gained range on top of the site already running. Technical illustrations show each product as architecture and flow. New colours tell product families apart. Sora and a monospace face bring the type closer to code. Tokens, a component library and documentation let product, documentation and support teams build and fix pages without waiting on design.

sections.body: A brand made for the people who write the code. Type that feels at home next to a terminal, and drawings that explain each product the way one developer would explain it to another.

items.title: Azion Console Kit
items.description: The screen engineers use to deploy and watch their applications, rebuilt from scratch. Vue 3, a shared component library, and an architecture that separates how a screen looks from what it does.
items.technologies: Vue 3, Vite, PrimeVue, TypeScript, Design Tokens, Component Architecture, Headless UI Pattern, Open Source
items.impact: Applications set up three times faster, 235% more new users becoming active, and a new screen in preview in about four hours. Open source: 6,000+ commits, 34+ contributors, 93+ releases. In production at Itaú, Magazine Luiza, iFood and Netshoes. Caio led it; the team he built wrote it.

sections.body: A full front-end rebuild of the console engineers at Itaú, Magazine Luiza and iFood use every day to deploy, secure and watch their applications.

sections.challenge: Every change in the console cost weeks, so interface work kept losing priority to the backend and each area of the product drifted into its own patterns. It showed most at the beginning, where someone who wanted to try the platform hit enough breaks in the journey to give up and wait for a salesperson.
sections.solution: A rebuild on Vue 3 over PrimeVue, an open component library, with Azion's own theme and blocks on top. Patterns were settled once and reused, so screens are assembled instead of hand-built. The flows people already knew stayed where they were, and the effort went into the first hour: templates, presets, import from GitHub and guidance inside the product, so a new user gets an application running without help.

sections.body: The old console sent you away to build anything: back to the menu, create the missing piece, find the way back. Now the missing piece opens where you are.

items.title: Azion Design System
items.description: The product had no shared kit of parts. Every team drew the same screen its own way, and the rules lived in a few people's heads. The system went in one screen at a time, so nobody woke up to a different-looking product.
items.technologies: Figma, Design Tokens, Zeroheight, Component Architecture, Roboto Typography, Semantic Color System, Iconography, Figma Plugins
items.impact: 40+ documented components on one foundation, built for the six or seven product teams consuming them, with a dedicated design and front-end team owning the system and the handoff. Published publicly at azion.design. It also settled a larger question: most of what looked like design debt was front-end architecture, and the evidence gathered screen by screen is what took the company to rebuilding that architecture.

sections.body: The design system behind the console customers use to run their applications: the first shared set of components, patterns and rules the product ever had.

sections.challenge: There was no documentation to build from. A team copied an existing screen and guessed the rest, so the same flow came out differently in each product. The rules lived with a handful of people: designers spent their time reviewing and correcting flows instead of designing, and a front-end engineer could not put an interface into production without one of them alongside.
sections.solution: Tokens, components, patterns and the documentation that says how to apply them, published at azion.design. Most screens were legacy, inside the monolith, so the system went in with the roadmap: whenever a product area was opened for a customer, its screens were rebuilt on the system and pulled into a modular architecture. A dedicated design and front-end team owned the system and the handoff to every product team.

items.title: Huia, Creativity & Innovation
items.description: Eight years at a creative technology studio in Porto Alegre: two running production squads, six as partner. The studio's job was to try what had never shipped in a campaign yet — 3D in the browser, a webcam that reads a pose — and make it work for brands like O Boticário, Petrobras and Tramontina.
items.technologies: WebGL, Three.js, GSAP, PoseNet, Machine learning, Motion design, Cinema 4D, After Effects, E-commerce platforms
items.impact: Creative and technical direction on 40+ projects. The coupon platform built for O Boticário kept 2,000+ stores in sync and raised store traffic by 30%. The studio went from a nucleus inside an agency to forty people selling applications directly to clients, and was acquired by Stefanini.

sections.body: Eight years of creative technology, and where Caio learned to carry an idea from the brief all the way into the code that runs it.

sections.challenge: Huia was born as a motion, video and technology nucleus spun out of the agency W3haus, and its brief was to try things nobody had shipped in a campaign yet. The risk in that work sits between the idea and the execution: an idea leaves the agency, passes through interface, 3D and code, and usually loses whatever made it good on the way.
sections.solution: Caio led both sides of it. He ran the interface and motion specialists and stayed with the development team until the work was live, so what reached the screen was still the idea that left the agency. Over the years he led the studio's shift from serving one agency to selling applications, tools, sites and brands directly to clients, which became its specialty.

philosophy.heading: Philosophy
philosophy.title: Fall, learn, evolve
philosophy.body:
Good design comes from the same place as good athleticism: a willingness to fail, learn, and go again.

Caio learned it on a judo mat. As he wrote in 2018: "In Judo, the first lessons are all focused on teaching how to fall. From the beginning, it's understood that you will fall, lose, err. So suffer less, lose the fear, preserve your body and, most importantly, prepare your mind for the obstacles ahead."

Skateboarding taught him the same thing. Skaters are the most persistent people he has met. They fall hundreds of times learning one trick, and do it without fear, because falling is the process rather than a failure of it.

It translates directly. The best work comes from teams that are not afraid to test, fail and change. Ship early, get it in front of people, keep going. Nothing good arrives finished.

Running a team, he tries to build places where people can fall safely. Where iterating is the point, not a setback. Where "I don't know yet" is a fine answer, as long as curiosity and action follow it.

lifestyle.heading: Life Outside Design
lifestyle.body:
I'm a triathlete, training 10-14 hours per week across running, cycling, and swimming. The discipline of athletic training—waking at 5 AM for a two-hour run, then putting in a full workday—teaches you to manage energy, focus on what matters, and push through discomfort.

Video games have been a lifelong passion and a major influence on my design work. I've always looked at games as inspiration—particularly for visual references and interaction design. The attention to detail in game UI/UX, the storytelling through visuals, and the immersive experiences have shaped how I approach digital product design.

Before design consumed my life, music did. I played bass in INFUSE, a melodic punk rock band. I'm a cinephile who watches every Oscar nominee each year (favorite directors: Tarantino, Wes Anderson, Almodovar, Scorsese, Nolan, Villeneuve).

I'm also a three-time Brazilian vice-champion in youth baseball categories, played volleyball at the state championship level at 17, and surfed for years. I'm an INTP—analytical, curious, always questioning. I work to balance my natural tendency to question everything with the need to ship and execute.

howHeWorks.heading: How he builds
howHeWorks.body:
He learned this on a judo mat, where the first lessons are about how to fall. You are going to fall, so you learn to do it without fear and carry on. Skateboarding taught him the same thing: a few hundred falls buy you one trick.

That is how he builds. Something rough goes up early, gets looked at, and changes. Nothing good arrives finished.

He works the whole span himself, from the idea to the way it looks to the code that puts it on screen. For a client that means one person carrying the work from the first thought to the thing being live, instead of a handoff between three.
